questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CuSO₄?
options: Copper(I) sulfate
Copper(II) sulfide
Copper(II) sulfite
Copper(II) sulfate
questions.explanation: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻, so copper must be Cu²⁺, shown by the Roman numeral II. Sulfide is S²⁻ and sulfite is SO₃²⁻.

questions.stem: What is the formula of iron(III) oxide?
options: FeO
Fe₃O
Fe₃O₂
Fe₂O₃
questions.explanation: Iron(III) is Fe³⁺ and oxide is O²⁻. Two Fe³⁺ (total +6) balance three O²⁻ (total −6), giving Fe₂O₃. FeO is iron(II) oxide.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of PCl₃?
options: Phosphorus trichloride
Phosphorus chloride
Phosphorus trichlorine
Triphosphorus chloride
questions.explanation: Binary covalent compounds of two non-metals use prefixes for the number of each atom: one phosphorus (no mono- on the first element) and three chlorines, so phosphorus trichloride.

questions.stem: What is the formula of ammonium carbonate?
options: (NH₄)₃CO₃
(NH₄)₂CO₃
NH₄CO₃
NH₄(CO₃)₂
questions.explanation: Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and carbonate is CO₃²⁻, so two ammonium ions are needed for each carbonate. Brackets show that the whole polyatomic ion is doubled.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of NaHCO₃?
options: Sodium hydrogen carbonate
Sodium carbonate
Sodium hydroxycarbonate
Sodium carbon hydride
questions.explanation: HCO₃⁻ is the hydrogen carbonate ion, so NaHCO₃ is sodium hydrogen carbonate, commonly called bicarbonate of soda. Sodium carbonate is Na₂CO₃.

questions.stem: Which statement describes metallic bonding?
options: Attraction between temporary dipoles on neighbouring metal atoms
Electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalised electrons
Electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions in a lattice
Sharing of electron pairs between neighbouring metal atoms in a network
questions.explanation: In a metal, the atoms release their valence electrons into a shared pool. The positive ions left behind are held in a lattice by their attraction to these delocalised electrons. Attraction between positive and negative ions is ionic bonding.

questions.stem: Why do solid metals conduct electricity?
options: Their positive ions can move through the lattice
Their atoms share electrons in fixed covalent bonds
Their ions are free to move once a voltage is applied
Their delocalised electrons move through the lattice
questions.explanation: An electric current is a flow of charge. In a metal the delocalised electrons are free to move when a voltage is applied, while the cations stay fixed in the lattice.

questions.stem: The boiling points of sodium (883 °C), magnesium (1090 °C) and aluminium (about 2500 °C) rise across period 3. Which explanation is best?
options: Each metal forms more covalent bonds between its atoms, as its electronegativity rises
Each metal has a larger atomic radius, so its atoms pack together more closely
Each atom gives more delocalised electrons and forms a smaller, more highly charged cation
Each metal has more electron shells, so there are more electrons to attract the cations
questions.explanation: Sodium gives one electron per atom, magnesium two and aluminium three, and the cations become smaller and more highly charged. The attraction between the cations and the delocalised electrons is stronger, so more energy is needed to separate the atoms.

questions.stem: In the model of a metal as layers of cations in a sea of delocalised electrons, why can the metal be hammered into a sheet without breaking?
options: The cations and electrons swap places, so the lattice reforms after each hammer blow
The layers can slide while the electrons keep attracting the cations in their new positions
The cations are repelled by the electrons, so the layers are pushed apart without breaking
The electrons form fixed bonds between pairs of cations, and these bonds bend without breaking
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is non-directional: wherever the cations move, they are still surrounded by delocalised electrons. Layers can therefore slide over one another and the metal changes shape instead of shattering.

questions.stem: Potassium melts at 63 °C and sodium at 98 °C. Both are in group 1. Why does potassium have the lower melting point?
options: Its cations have a higher charge, so they repel each other more strongly
It has fewer protons, so its cations attract the delocalised electrons less
It gives more delocalised electrons per atom, which push the cations apart
Its cations are larger, so they attract the delocalised electrons less
questions.explanation: Both metals give one electron per atom and form 1+ ions, but K⁺ has an extra shell and is larger. Its charge is spread over a larger ion, so the attraction to the delocalised electrons is weaker. Potassium has more protons (19) than sodium (11).

questions.stem: Using the electronegativities given in brackets, which pair of elements is most likely to form an ionic bond?
options: Na (0.9) and Cl (3.2)
questions.explanation: A large difference in electronegativity means one atom takes the electrons completely, forming ions. Sodium and chlorine differ by 2.3, while the other pairs differ by 0.8 or less and form covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Magnesium and nitrogen react to form an ionic compound. What is its formula?
options: Mg₃N₂
MgN
Mg₂N₃
MgN₂
questions.explanation: Magnesium is in group 2 and forms Mg²⁺, and nitrogen is in group 15 and forms N³⁻. Three Mg²⁺ (+6) balance two N³⁻ (−6), giving Mg₃N₂.

questions.stem: How are the ions arranged in a solid ionic compound such as sodium chloride?
options: Each ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge in a repeating 3D lattice
The ions exist as separate pairs, each Na⁺ bonded to just one particular Cl⁻ ion
Ions of the same charge sit next to each other in alternating flat layers
The ions move freely past each other, held together by delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: An ionic solid is a lattice: in sodium chloride each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ and each Cl⁻ by six Na⁺. There are no separate NaCl molecules, and ions of like charge are kept apart.

questions.stem: A white solid melts at 770 °C. It does not conduct electricity as a solid, but its solution in water does. What type of bonding is present?
options: Covalent molecular
Covalent network
Ionic
Metallic
questions.explanation: A high melting point with conduction only when dissolved or molten is typical of an ionic compound: the ions are fixed in the solid but free to move in solution. A metal would conduct as a solid, and covalent substances do not form ions in this way.

questions.stem: Melting points of group 1 chlorides are NaCl 801 °C, KCl 771 °C, RbCl 715 °C and CsCl 646 °C. Which explanation fits this trend?
options: The chloride ion gets larger down the group, so it is held less strongly by the cation
The cation gets larger down the group, so the attraction between the ions weakens
The cation charge rises down the group, so the ions repel each other more strongly
The bonds become more covalent down the group as the metal's electronegativity rises
questions.explanation: Down group 1 the cation gains a shell each time, so the distance between the centres of oppositely charged ions increases and the electrostatic attraction weakens. The chloride ion is the same in every compound, and every cation has a 1+ charge.

questions.stem: Beryllium chloride melts at about 400 °C, far lower than magnesium chloride (714 °C) and calcium chloride (772 °C). Which explanation is best?
options: Beryllium ions are larger than other group 2 ions, so they attract chloride ions more weakly
Beryllium has a 1+ charge in this compound, so its ionic bonds are only half as strong
Beryllium chloride is a covalent network, and networks melt at lower temperatures than ionic solids
The small electronegativity difference between Be and Cl makes the bonding largely covalent
questions.explanation: Beryllium is the most electronegative group 2 metal, and its tiny ion pulls strongly on the chloride's electrons, so the bonding is largely covalent rather than ionic. Weaker forces between the units mean a much lower melting point. Be²⁺ is the smallest group 2 ion, not the largest.

questions.stem: Magnesium oxide melts at about 2800 °C, but sodium fluoride melts at about 1000 °C. The ions in both have 10 electrons and are arranged in the same type of lattice. Why is the difference so large?
options: Fluoride is more electronegative than oxide, so it weakens the ionic bond
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges, so they attract each other much more strongly
Magnesium oxide is a covalent network, while sodium fluoride is an ionic lattice
Magnesium oxide contains delocalised electrons that strengthen the lattice
questions.explanation: The attraction between ions increases with the size of their charges. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ each carry twice the charge of Na⁺ and F⁻, so the ionic bonding in magnesium oxide is much stronger. The smaller size of Mg²⁺ adds to the effect.

questions.stem: What holds two atoms together in a covalent bond?
options: A pool of delocalised electrons around both atoms
Temporary dipoles induced in the two atoms' electrons
A shared pair of electrons attracted to both nuclei
The attraction between two oppositely charged ions
questions.explanation: In a covalent bond the two nuclei are both attracted to the electron pair they share, which holds them together. Attraction between oppositely charged ions is ionic bonding.

questions.stem: Silicon dioxide melts above 1600 °C, while carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature. Why?
options: SiO₂ is an ionic lattice, while CO₂ is a covalent network
SiO₂ has hydrogen bonds between molecules, while CO₂ has dispersion forces
SiO₂ has double bonds, while CO₂ has weaker single bonds between atoms
SiO₂ is a covalent network, while CO₂ is made of separate molecules
questions.explanation: In silicon dioxide every atom is joined to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds throughout the solid, so melting means breaking bonds. Carbon dioxide molecules are held to each other only by weak dispersion forces.

questions.stem: How many lone pairs of electrons are on the oxygen atom in the electron dot diagram of the hydroxide ion, OH⁻?
questions.explanation: Oxygen brings six valence electrons, hydrogen one, and the negative charge one more, giving eight. Two are in the O-H bond, leaving six as three lone pairs on the oxygen.

questions.stem: How many lone pairs of electrons are on the nitrogen atom in the electron dot diagram of the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen's five valence electrons, plus four from the hydrogens, minus one for the positive charge, give eight electrons: four bonding pairs. Ammonia, NH₃, has one lone pair, but in NH₄⁺ that pair forms the fourth N-H bond.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons in total are shown in the electron dot diagram of the acetate (ethanoate) ion, CH₃COO⁻?
questions.explanation: Two carbons give 2 × 4 = 8, three hydrogens give 3 and two oxygens give 2 × 6 = 12, totalling 23. The 1− charge adds one more electron, giving 24. Forgetting the charge gives 23.

questions.stem: Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen. Which statement describes the H-Cl bond?
options: It is polar, with a partial negative charge on the hydrogen atom
It is ionic, with chlorine taking the hydrogen's electron completely
It is non-polar, because the electrons are shared between the atoms
It is polar, with a partial negative charge on the chlorine atom
questions.explanation: The more electronegative chlorine pulls the shared pair towards itself, giving it a partial negative charge (δ−) and leaving hydrogen δ+. The difference is not large enough for full electron transfer.

questions.stem: Boron trifluoride, BF₃, has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs around boron. What is its shape?
options: Trigonal planar
Trigonal pyramidal
Tetrahedral
Bent
questions.explanation: Three electron groups repel each other to be as far apart as possible, 120° apart in a flat triangle. A trigonal pyramidal shape needs a fourth electron group, a lone pair, as in NH₃.

questions.stem: What are the shape and polarity of a hydrogen sulfide molecule, H₂S?
options: Linear and polar
Bent and polar
Linear and non-polar
Bent and non-polar
questions.explanation: Sulfur has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, so like water the molecule is bent. The S-H bonds are polar and, because of the bent shape, their dipoles do not cancel.

questions.stem: What are the shape and polarity of hydrogen cyanide, H-C≡N?
options: Linear and polar
Bent and polar
Linear and non-polar
Trigonal planar and polar
questions.explanation: Carbon has two electron groups (the single bond and the triple bond) and no lone pairs, so the molecule is linear. Nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the dipoles point the same way and do not cancel.

questions.stem: BF₃ is non-polar, but NH₃ is polar, although both have three polar bonds. Which explanation is correct?
options: BF₃ has a lone pair that makes it flat, so its bond dipoles cancel each other out
N-H bonds are polar but B-F bonds are not, because fluorine and boron are similar
NH₃ forms hydrogen bonds within each molecule, which make the molecule polar
NH₃ has a lone pair that makes it pyramidal, so its bond dipoles do not cancel
questions.explanation: In BF₃ the three bond dipoles lie 120° apart in a plane and cancel. The lone pair on nitrogen makes NH₃ pyramidal, so its dipoles add to give an overall dipole. B-F bonds are in fact very polar.

questions.stem: What are the shape and polarity of dichloromethane, CH₂Cl₂?
options: Tetrahedral and non-polar
Trigonal pyramidal and polar
Tetrahedral and polar
Square planar and non-polar
questions.explanation: Carbon has four bonding pairs, so the molecule is tetrahedral, not flat as it looks when drawn on paper. The C-Cl and C-H bonds have different polarities, so the dipoles do not cancel and the molecule is polar.

questions.stem: Hydrogen bonds form between molecules in which a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to:
options: any non-metal atom at all
carbon, nitrogen or oxygen
chlorine, bromine or iodine
nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine
questions.explanation: Nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine are small and highly electronegative, so the H atom bonded to them is strongly δ+ and is attracted to a lone pair on a neighbouring molecule. C-H bonds are not polar enough.

questions.stem: Propane (C₃H₈, 44 g mol⁻¹) boils at −42 °C, while ethanal (CH₃CHO, 44 g mol⁻¹) boils at 20 °C. Which explains the difference?
options: Propane has weaker covalent bonds, which break more easily when it boils
Ethanal is polar, so it has dipole-dipole forces as well as dispersion forces
Ethanal forms hydrogen bonds because it contains both hydrogen and oxygen atoms
Ethanal has more electrons, so its dispersion forces are much stronger
questions.explanation: The two molecules have similar numbers of electrons, so similar dispersion forces. Ethanal's polar C=O group adds dipole-dipole attraction. It cannot hydrogen bond with itself, because its hydrogens are bonded to carbon, not oxygen.

questions.stem: Boiling points are HF 20 °C, HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C and HI −35 °C. Which statement explains this pattern?
options: HF forms hydrogen bonds; from HCl to HI dispersion forces increase with more electrons
HF has the most electrons; from HCl to HI the dipole-dipole forces become stronger
HF has the strongest covalent bond; from HCl to HI the bonds become weaker
HF is ionic; from HCl to HI the molecules become more polar and attract more
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding between HF molecules gives it by far the highest boiling point. From HCl to HI the molecules have more electrons, so dispersion forces grow, outweighing the falling polarity. Boiling does not break covalent bonds.

questions.stem: How do dispersion forces arise between non-polar molecules?
options: Temporary uneven electron distributions create dipoles that induce dipoles in neighbours
Permanent partial charges on polar bonds attract opposite charges on neighbours
Hydrogen atoms on one molecule are attracted to lone pairs on another molecule
Electrons are transferred between molecules, leaving them oppositely charged
questions.explanation: At any instant the electrons in a molecule may be unevenly spread, forming a temporary dipole. This induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule, and the two attract. Permanent partial charges cause dipole-dipole forces.

questions.stem: For small molecules of similar size, which lists these from strongest to weakest?
options: Covalent bond, hydrogen bond, dipole-dipole force, dispersion force
Hydrogen bond, covalent bond, dipole-dipole force, dispersion force
Covalent bond, dipole-dipole force, hydrogen bond, dispersion force
Dispersion force, dipole-dipole force, hydrogen bond, covalent bond
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds within molecules are much stronger than any intermolecular force. Among intermolecular forces for molecules of similar size, hydrogen bonds are strongest, then dipole-dipole forces, then dispersion forces.

questions.stem: Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) boils at 78 °C, but methoxymethane (CH₃OCH₃), with the same molecular formula, boils at −24 °C. Why?
options: Ethanol has stronger C-H bonds, which take more energy to break on boiling
Ethanol has an O-H group, so its molecules hydrogen bond to each other
Methoxymethane has fewer electrons, so its dispersion forces are much weaker
Methoxymethane is non-polar because its oxygen atom has no lone pairs
questions.explanation: Both have the formula C₂H₆O and the same number of electrons. Only ethanol has a hydrogen bonded to oxygen, so only ethanol molecules hydrogen bond with one another. Methoxymethane's hydrogens are all bonded to carbon.

questions.stem: When solid iodine, I₂, sublimes to a purple gas, what is overcome?
options: Hydrogen bonds between I₂ molecules
Ionic bonds between I⁺ and I⁻ ions
Dispersion forces between I₂ molecules
Covalent bonds between iodine atoms
questions.explanation: Iodine is a molecular substance, so changing state separates whole I₂ molecules from each other. The I-I covalent bond stays intact, and non-polar I₂ molecules are held only by dispersion forces.

questions.stem: A substance melts above 1600 °C, is very hard and does not conduct electricity as a solid or a liquid. What type of structure does it have?
options: Covalent network
Ionic lattice
Metallic lattice
Covalent molecular
questions.explanation: A very high melting point and hardness show strong bonds throughout the solid, and no conduction even when molten rules out ions and delocalised electrons. An ionic compound would conduct when molten.

questions.stem: A ball-and-stick model of sodium chloride shows sticks joining each ion to its neighbours. What is a limitation of this model?
options: The model shows a repeating pattern, but ions in a solid are arranged at random
The sticks show that ions share electron pairs, which ions in a lattice really do
The sticks suggest fixed bonds between particular ions, but ionic bonding is non-directional
The model shows the ions as spheres, but ions in a lattice are actually flat discs
questions.explanation: Each ion is attracted equally in all directions to every nearby ion of opposite charge, so there are no individual bonds for the sticks to represent. The model is useful for showing the arrangement of ions in the lattice.

questions.stem: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms from graphite. Why does it conduct electricity?
options: Dispersion forces between the carbon atoms allow electrons to jump across
Each carbon bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom
Each carbon bonds to four others, so electrons pass along the covalent bonds
The layer contains carbon ions that move when a voltage is applied
questions.explanation: In graphene, as in each layer of graphite, every carbon atom uses three electrons in covalent bonds. The fourth is delocalised across the sheet and can move when a voltage is applied.

questions.stem: Diamond and graphite are both forms of pure carbon. Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
options: All four outer electrons of each carbon are held in localised covalent bonds
Its carbon atoms are held together by weak dispersion forces only
Its carbon atoms form positive ions that are fixed in place in the lattice
Its electrons are delocalised between layers that cannot slide past each other
questions.explanation: Each carbon in diamond is covalently bonded to four others in a tetrahedral network, so no electrons are free to move. In graphite each carbon bonds to only three, leaving one delocalised electron.

questions.stem: Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, is much softer than diamond and changes state at a much lower temperature. Which explanation is correct?
options: It is made of separate C₆₀ molecules held together by dispersion forces
Its carbon atoms are joined by ionic bonds, which are weaker than covalent ones
It is a covalent network like diamond, but each carbon has only two bonds
Its layers of carbon atoms are held together by hydrogen bonds that break easily
questions.explanation: C₆₀ is a covalent molecular substance: the bonds within each cage are strong, but separate cages are held only by dispersion forces. Diamond is a continuous network, so changing its state means breaking covalent bonds.
